claims.text: Changing individual elemental percentages in HfNbTaTiZr will produce systematic and measurable changes in mechanical properties.
The initial material is an equiatomic or near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy exhibits characteristic high-entropy behavior.
Combinatorial sputtering can fabricate compositionally graded HfNbTaTiZr thin-film libraries.
The percentages of Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr can be systematically varied across such sputtered libraries.
Nanoindentation or microscale tensile testing can spatially measure the mechanical properties of the compositionally graded library.
Non-equiatomic compositions will cause local variations in phase structure and grain size.
Changing elemental percentages alters lattice distortion and elemental mixing.
Changing individual elemental percentages alters lattice distortion and phase stability.
Changes in lattice distortion and phase stability modulate dislocation movement.
Modulation of dislocation movement produces variations in hardness and strength.
Grain refinement in HfNbTaTiZr can be associated with high hardness.
Increasing Hf content may increase hardness or alter elastic modulus relative to an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr baseline.
Increasing Ta content may increase hardness or alter elastic modulus relative to an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr baseline.
Other compositional shifts may reduce hardness or elastic modulus.
The direction and magnitude of mechanical-property changes depend on how each element modifies the local microstructure.
Processing route and microstructural evolution can influence the mechanical properties of HfNbTaTiZr.
Mechanical properties from thin-film HfNbTaTiZr studies may not directly translate to bulk material because of processing and scale effects.
An equiatomic or near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr sample prepared under similar conditions should serve as the baseline control.
Absence of a systematic composition–property correlation after accounting for processing-induced microstructural differences would falsify the hypothesis.
